lessons.title: Glass Composition and Properties
lessons.body:
Glass is made by melting silica sand (SiOâ), soda ash (NaâCOâ), and limestone (CaCOâ) at about 1,500Â°C. In Africa, silica sand is abundant in countries like Kenya, South Africa, and Nigeria. Soda ash is mined in Kenya (Lake Magadi) and Botswana. Limestone is widespread. The typical recipe: 70-75% silica sand, 12-15% soda ash, 10-15% limestone, plus small amounts of cullet (recycled glass) and decolorizers. Cullet lowers melting energy and is essential for recycling.

Key properties for packaging: glass is chemically inert, impermeable to gases and liquids, and can be sterilized. It is brittle but strong under compression. Density is about 2.5 g/cmÂ³. Thermal expansion coefficient matters for thermal shock resistance; borosilicate glass (like Pyrex) expands less and resists sudden temperature changes better than soda-lime glass. In Africa, most beverage bottles are soda-lime glass.

Practical testing: To check if glass is soda-lime, scratch it with a steel file; it will scratch. Borosilicate is harder. To test thermal shock, heat a sample in water to 80Â°C, then plunge into ice water; soda-lime may crack, borosilicate will not. For packaging, you want glass that survives pasteurization (up to 85Â°C) and transport over rough roads.

In Africa, local glass production uses recycled cullet from informal collectors. For example, in Nigeria, the Ogba glass plant uses up to 80% cullet. A small-scale producer can buy cullet from waste pickers at about $50-100 per tonne. Sorting by colour is critical: clear, green, and amber must be kept separate to avoid colour contamination. Green glass is common for beer and wine; amber protects against UV light.

When starting a glass packaging business, source silica sand from local rivers or quarries, ensure it is low in iron (less than 0.1% FeâOâ) for clear glass. Iron gives green colour. Soda ash can be purchased from chemical suppliers or imported. Limestone should be crushed to less than 2 mm. Mix thoroughly before melting. Remember: glass composition affects strength, colour, and chemical resistance. A simple batch formula for 100 kg: 72 kg silica sand, 14 kg soda ash, 12 kg limestone, 2 kg cullet. Adjust based on local materials.

lessons.title: Glass Container Manufacturing: Blow and Press-Blow
lessons.body:
Two main methods make glass containers: blow-and-blow for narrow-mouth bottles (beer, soda), and press-blow for wide-mouth jars (jam, mayonnaise). Both start with a gob of molten glass at about 1,100Â°C cut by shears and dropped into a blank mould.

Blow-and-blow: In the blank mould, compressed air (0.2-0.5 bar) blows a parison (pre-shape). The parison is inverted into the blow mould, then high-pressure air (2-4 bar) expands it to final shape. This method is used for bottles with neck diameter less than 50 mm. Cycle time: 10-20 seconds per bottle. A typical IS machine (Individual Section) has 6-12 sections, producing 50-200 bottles per minute.

Press-blow: A metal plunger presses the gob into the blank mould to form the parison, then air blows it in the blow mould. This is for wide-mouth containers (diameter >50 mm). The plunger leaves a mark inside the jar, which is acceptable. Press-blow is faster for jars: 30-60 jars per minute.

In Africa, small-scale glassworks often use semi-automatic machines. For example, in Egypt, some factories use Lynch machines. But for a start-up, you can buy a used IS machine from China or India for $20,000-$50,000. You also need a furnace (continuous melting tank), forehearth, and annealing lehr. A small furnace melts 5-10 tonnes per day. Fuel: natural gas or heavy fuel oil. In Nigeria, gas is cheaper; in Kenya, electricity for electric furnaces.

Practical tips: Keep moulds clean and lubricated with a graphite-based swabbing compound. Mould temperature should be 400-500Â°C for blank, 350-450Â°C for blow. Glass temperature at gob: 1,050-1,150Â°C. If glass is too cold, it will not blow; too hot, it will stick to mould. Use a pyrometer to check. For a small operation, you can start with a single-section machine and 2-3 workers per shift. Training is available from machine suppliers. Remember: blow-and-blow for bottles, press-blow for jars. Test your first bottles for wall thickness (should be 2-4 mm) and capacity (fill with water to check volume).

lessons.title: Design and Finishes for Glass Containers
lessons.body:
Glass container design affects strength, filling speed, and shelf appeal. Key dimensions: body diameter, height, neck finish, and weight. Standard bottle finishes are defined by GCMI (Glass Container Manufacturers Institute) and ISO. For Africa, common finishes: crown cap (26 mm for beer), screw cap (28 mm for soda, 38 mm for juice), and lug cap (for jam jars).

Neck finish: The top part where the closure fits. It has threads or lugs. For crown caps, the finish is a lip (crown finish) with a diameter of 26.75 mm. For screw caps, threads per inch (TPI) matter: 28 mm finish has 1.5 threads per mm. Always specify finish code, e.g., 26-610 for crown. In Africa, many small producers use imported pre-made bottles because making your own finish requires precise moulds.

Design rules: Avoid sharp corners; use rounded shoulders and bases. Wall thickness should be uniform: 2-4 mm for body, 3-5 mm at base. The base should have a push-up (concave) to resist internal pressure. For carbonated drinks, pressure can reach 4-6 bar; bottles must be tested to 10 bar. Weight: a 330 ml beer bottle weighs 180-220 g. Lighter bottles save glass but are weaker.

Practical: To design a bottle, draw it on paper with dimensions. Then make a wooden or metal model. Test with a 3D printer if available. For moulds, you need cast iron or bronze. In Africa, mould makers in South Africa and Egypt can produce moulds for $2,000-$5,000 per mould. Alternatively, buy standard moulds from China. Always include a mould number and date code on the bottom for traceability.

Finishes for closures: Crown caps need a lip with a diameter of 26.75 mm and a height of 6.5 mm. Screw caps need threads that match the cap. For a 28 mm screw cap, the finish has a 28 mm outer diameter and 1.5 mm pitch. Test closure fit by hand: cap should screw on smoothly and not leak. Fill bottle with water, invert, and squeeze; no leaks. For lug caps (twist-off), the finish has 4 lugs; cap turns 1/4 turn to seal. In Africa, many jams and sauces use lug caps. Ensure your finish matches locally available closures to avoid import costs.

lessons.title: Closures and Sealing Systems for Glass
lessons.body:
Closures seal the bottle and protect contents. Main types: crown caps (metal), screw caps (metal or plastic), lug caps (metal), and cork (for wine). In Africa, crown caps are ubiquitous for beer and soda. They are made of tinplate or aluminium, lined with PVC or EVA gasket. A crown cap costs $0.01-$0.03. Screw caps for spirits and juices cost $0.05-$0.15. Lug caps for jam cost $0.08-$0.20.

Sealing mechanism: Crown caps crimp onto the bottle lip. The gasket deforms to create a seal. For carbonated drinks, the cap must hold 4-6 bar. Test by filling with carbonated water, capping, and storing at 40Â°C for 24 hours; no leaks. Screw caps use a thread and a liner (foam or plastisol) to seal. Lug caps have a lug that engages with the bottle finish; a plastisol liner seals.

Application tools: Manual crown capper ($50-$150) for small scale; pneumatic capper ($500-$2,000) for medium. For screw caps, a manual capping machine ($200-$500) or automatic ($5,000+). In Africa, many small breweries use manual cappers. For lug caps, a steam capper is needed to soften the plastisol; a simple steam pot works.

Practical tips: Store closures in a dry place; moisture ruins gaskets. Check cap dimensions: crown cap inner diameter should be 26.75 mm. For screw caps, match thread pitch. Test seal integrity by submerging capped bottle in water and looking for bubbles (leak test). For pasteurized products, use heat-resistant liners. In Africa, import closures from China or South Africa; local production is limited but growing in Nigeria and Kenya. Consider buying in bulk (10,000 units) to reduce cost. Always keep a spare capping head. Train workers to cap consistently: too tight cracks the neck, too loose leaks. Use a torque tester for screw caps: 1.5-2.5 Nm for 28 mm. For crown caps, crimp diameter should be 26.5-27.0 mm.

lessons.title: Annealing and Strengthening of Glass
lessons.body:
After forming, glass cools rapidly and develops internal stresses. Annealing removes these stresses by reheating to about 550Â°C (annealing point) and slowly cooling. This is done in a lehr (annealing oven). A lehr is a tunnel with zones: heating, soaking, and cooling. Glass enters at 500-600Â°C, moves through at 1-2 m/min, and exits at 50-80Â°C. Total time: 30-60 minutes. Without annealing, bottles crack easily.

In Africa, small producers can build a simple lehr with firebricks and a conveyor belt. Or buy a used lehr for $5,000-$20,000. Fuel: gas or electricity. Temperature control is critical: use thermocouples and a controller. If glass cools too fast, it breaks; too slow, it wastes energy. Test annealing quality by polariscope: a stressed bottle shows coloured bands. A well-annealed bottle shows uniform dark field.

Strengthening: Two methods: thermal tempering and chemical strengthening. Thermal tempering: heat glass to 600-700Â°C, then blast with air. This creates compressive stress on surfaces, making it 4-5 times stronger. Used for beer bottles in some markets. Chemical strengthening: dip glass in molten potassium nitrate at 400-450Â°C for hours; potassium ions replace sodium ions, creating compressive stress. This is expensive and rare in Africa. Most African bottles are only annealed, not tempered.

Practical: For a start-up, focus on proper annealing. Build a lehr with a 5 m tunnel, 1 m wide. Use a conveyor chain. Heat with gas burners. Control speed with a variable speed motor. Test bottles by dropping from 1 m onto concrete; annealed bottles may break, but well-annealed ones break into larger pieces, not shards. For strengthening, you can hot-fill bottles with hot water (80Â°C) and let cool slowly to reduce stress. Also, avoid scratches: handle bottles gently. In Africa, recycled bottles often have scratches, reducing strength. Inspect and reject scratched bottles. Use a simple polariscope (two polarizing films) to check annealing. If you see rainbow colours, re-anneal.

lessons.title: Inspection and Defect Analysis in Glass Packaging
lessons.body:
Defects cost money. Common defects: stones (unmelted sand), cords (streaks), bubbles, cracks, chipped finish, and thin walls. Inspection starts with visual checks on the production line. In Africa, many small factories use manual inspectors with good lighting. A simple inspection station: a table with a bright light and a rotating stand. Inspect every bottle for: cracks (especially at neck and base), chipped finish (run finger around lip), and foreign matter.

Tools: Polariscope for stress, micrometer for wall thickness, go/no-go gauges for finish dimensions, and a pressure tester for carbonated bottles. A pressure tester is a simple hand pump with a gauge; fill bottle with water, pressurize to 10 bar, hold for 1 minute. No leaks or bursts. For finish, use a caliper: crown finish diameter should be 26.75 Â±0.2 mm. For wall thickness, use an ultrasonic thickness gauge ($200-$500) or break a bottle and measure with a micrometer.

Defect analysis: If you see bubbles, check furnace temperature (too low) or cullet quality (too much moisture). Stones mean unmelted batch; increase melting time or reduce grain size. Cords indicate poor mixing; improve batch mixing. Cracks often come from rapid cooling in lehr; slow down lehr speed. Chipped finish from rough handling; check conveyor transfers. Thin walls from uneven gob weight; adjust gob cutter.

In Africa, a common defect is
due to low blow pressure. Increase air pressure. Another is

(thin glass strand inside) from a dirty mould; clean moulds. For recycled glass, defects like scratches and chips are common; sort carefully. Implement a quality control log: record defect type, time, and machine. Use Pareto analysis: 80% of defects come from 20% of causes. Train workers to identify defects. A simple acceptance sampling plan: inspect 50 bottles per hour; if more than 2 defective, stop and adjust. Remember: a defective bottle can cause injury or product loss. Always test a sample from each batch for pressure and thermal shock. For thermal shock, heat bottle in water to 80Â°C, then plunge into ice water; no cracks means good annealing. Keep records for traceability.

quiz.q: What is the main ingredient in glass?
quiz.explanation: Silica sand (SiOâ) makes up 70-75% of glass batch.

quiz.q: Which country in Africa is a major source of soda ash?
quiz.explanation: Kenya mines soda ash at Lake Magadi.

quiz.q: What is cullet?
quiz.explanation: Cullet is crushed recycled glass used in the batch.

quiz.q: Which glass type is more resistant to thermal shock?
quiz.explanation: Borosilicate has a lower thermal expansion coefficient.

quiz.q: What is the typical melting temperature of glass?
quiz.explanation: Glass melts at about 1,500Â°C.

quiz.q: Which method is used for narrow-mouth bottles?
quiz.explanation: Blow-and-blow is for bottles with neck diameter <50 mm.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the blank mould?
options: A) To form the final shape
quiz.explanation: The blank mould shapes the gob into a parison.

quiz.q: Which machine is commonly used for glass container production?
quiz.explanation: IS (Individual Section) machines are standard for glass containers.

quiz.q: What is the typical cycle time for blow-and-blow?
quiz.explanation: Cycle time is 10-20 seconds per bottle.

quiz.q: What is the gob temperature before forming?
quiz.explanation: Gob temperature is about 1,100Â°C.

quiz.q: Which finish is used for crown caps?
quiz.explanation: Crown caps use a 26 mm crown finish.

quiz.q: What does GCMI stand for?
options: C) Glass Composition and Materials Institute
quiz.explanation: GCMI sets standard finishes for glass containers.

quiz.q: What is a push-up on a bottle base?
quiz.explanation: Push-up is a concave base that resists internal pressure.

quiz.q: What is the typical wall thickness for a glass bottle?
quiz.explanation: Wall thickness is usually 2-4 mm for body.

quiz.q: Which closure is common for jam jars?
quiz.explanation: Lug caps (twist-off) are used for jam jars.

quiz.q: What is the function of a gasket in a closure?
quiz.explanation: The gasket deforms to create a seal.

quiz.q: What is the typical pressure a carbonated beverage bottle must hold?
quiz.explanation: Carbonated drinks can reach 4-6 bar.

quiz.q: Which tool is used to test closure torque?
quiz.explanation: Torque tester measures the force to unscrew a cap.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of annealing?
quiz.explanation: Annealing removes stresses from rapid cooling.

quiz.q: What is the annealing temperature for glass?
quiz.explanation: Glass is annealed at about 550Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a lehr?
quiz.explanation: A lehr is a tunnel oven for annealing.

quiz.q: How can you check annealing quality?
quiz.explanation: Polariscope shows stress patterns in glass.

quiz.q: What is thermal tempering?
quiz.explanation: Thermal tempering uses air blasts to create compressive stress.

quiz.q: Which defect is caused by unmelted batch?
quiz.explanation: Stones are unmelted sand or batch particles.

quiz.q: What causes bubbles in glass?
quiz.explanation: Bubbles form when glass is too cold to release gases.

quiz.q: What is a common defect in recycled glass?
quiz.explanation: Recycled bottles often have scratches from handling.

quiz.q: Which gauge checks finish dimensions?
quiz.explanation: Go/no-go gauges quickly check if finish meets size.

quiz.q: What is the first step in defect analysis?
options: A) Record defect type and time
quiz.explanation: Recording defects helps identify patterns.

quiz.q: What does a pressure tester do?
options: B) Tests bottle strength under pressure
quiz.explanation: Pressure tester pressurizes bottle to check for leaks or bursts.

quiz.q: What is the typical acceptance sampling for small factories?
quiz.explanation: Inspecting 50 bottles per hour is practical for small-scale.
